title: Passover: Elijah's cup
hook: a cup is poured for Elijah and the door is opened

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's line, in every generation. Your line was as if you left. Did you tell part of your story in the present tense? Tonight, someone else is expected at the table. Day six hundred eighty-two.

It's late. The meal is over, the grace after meals is said, and the children are fading. Then someone fills a large, often beautiful cup that's been sitting untouched all night. A child is sent to open the front door. Cold air comes in. Everyone stands, or goes quiet, or sings. And the youngest kids watch the cup very closely, absolutely certain that if they look hard enough, they'll see the wine go down a little. Nobody at the table has invited this guest. He's been expected for a very long time.
screen: `A CUP UNTOUCHED ALL NIGHT.` → `A CHILD OPENS THE DOOR.` → `WATCHING THE WINE.`

segments.voice: The guest is Elijah, the prophet. In the book of Kings, the text never says he dies; he's carried up to heaven in a whirlwind, with a chariot of fire. So in Jewish tradition, he never quite left. He turns up in Talmudic stories, disguised as a traveler, a beggar, a merchant. And Malachi, whose book closes the Prophets, ends with a promise: God will send Elijah before the great day of the LORD. In the old Jewish translation: "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." So Elijah became the messenger of redemption. Why a cup? One explanation goes back to an old question: are there four cups at the seder, or five? Some versions of the Talmud mention a fifth. A popular later explanation says that since the question was never settled, a fifth cup is poured and not drunk, and it's named for Elijah, who, tradition says, will one day answer the questions the rabbis left open. Why open the door? It's opened right before a passage asking God to pour out wrath on the nations that devoured Israel, words from the Psalms, said in years of real persecution. The Torah also calls this night a night of watching, so some explain there's nothing to fear in opening the door. And Elijah, if he's coming, should find it open. More recently, some families have added a cup of water for Miriam, the prophet, beside Elijah's. Other families keep the older custom alone. Either way, the seder doesn't end with the door shut. It ends with it open, waiting.
screen: `ELIJAH NEVER DIED.` · `TURN THE HEARTS, MALACHI SAYS.` · `A FIFTH CUP, NOT DRUNK.` · `A NIGHT OF WATCHING.` · then, large: `LEAVE THE DOOR OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a door for a minute. If you can, get up now and open a door or a window. Feel the air change. Stand there and breathe. Think of what you're waiting for: a reconciliation, a recovery, a turn in the world, a guest you haven't met yet. Malachi's promise was about hearts turning toward each other, parents to children, children to parents. Is there one heart you'd like turned toward you, or yours toward them? Leave the door open while you sit. The bell holds the time.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, and a night that ends with Elijah's cup poured and the door left open. Today's word.
Your line: leave the door open. Today, leave one small opening for someone: a message, an invitation, a seat. Day six hundred eighty-two.

fork.setup: the rabbis can't decide whether the seder has four cups or five. the question was never settled. what does the tradition do?
options: drink four, and leave it there.
pour a fifth, name it for Elijah, and don't drink it.
fork.reveal: a fifth cup is poured for Elijah, who, tradition says, will one day answer the questions the rabbis left open.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cup for a ghostly visitor.
what it means: a cup for the messenger of redemption, and an open door for hope.
what a scholar hears: 2 Kings 2, Malachi 3:23–24, a variant in Pesachim 118a mentioning a fifth cup, and the night of watching in Exodus 12:42.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut "two and a half thousand years"; the text never says Elijah does not die, so the voice now says the text never says he dies; Malachi is the book that closes the Prophets, not "the last prophet in the Hebrew Bible"; softened "many say" and "recent decades".
Malachi 3:24 (JPS numbering; 4:6 in Christian Bibles) quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Pesachim 118a: some manuscripts/versions read 'on the fifth cup one says the Great Hallel'; the link between the fifth cup and Elijah resolving disputes is a later explanation. Verify.
Door opened at 'Shfoch chamatcha' (Psalm 79:6–7 and other verses); 'leil shimurim' (Exodus 12:42) as the reason no fear is needed: later explanations. Check.
'Two and a half thousand years' refers to Malachi (c. 5th century BCE); approximate.
Reviewer edit: the fifth-cup-for-Elijah explanation is now framed as a popular later explanation, not settled history.
Miriam's cup: a custom from the late 20th century; stated without judgment.
